On the orders of the day:

In view of the widespread starvation in Europe will the Acting Prime Minister tell the house what further steps the government intends to take to avert needless human suffering caused by lack of food in Europe?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The	Canadian government has
made it clear on a number of occasions that it recognizes the urgency of the food situation in Europe and Asia and that it is prepared to cooperate, and is cooperating, with the United Kingdom, the United States and other nations in making additional food available for shipment abroad. Without in any way detracting from the efforts of other countries, I think it is recognized that the people of Canada have made and are making a notable contribution to the relief of hunger and starvation the world over. The question asked by my hon. friend relates to the further steps the government intends to take. My answer can only be this: that the Canadian government intends to continue its present policy of cooperation with other governments in providing food so that hunger and starvation will be minimized if they cannot be averted. If this cooperation involves measures in addition to those already taken, they will be announced in due course.

Canadian Citizenship

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS

speechtext: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Secretary of State) moved the third reading of bill No. 7, respecting citizenship, nationality and naturalization and status of aliens.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
Before the motion is put there are two or three observations I should like to make in regard to the meaning of citizenship. Speaking to the amendment which I moved in committee on May 7, I said, as reported at page 1300 of Hansard:
This amendment is not meant to be allexclusive, nor is it meant to be all-inclusive. My first suggestion is that if the Secretary of State accepts the principle of the need in this country of a bill of rights signifying what citizenship stands for, then possibly the best means whereby that result could be effected would be to set up a committee of the house. It ivould not take very long for that committee to meet and it would afford an opportunity to exchange ideas among the various groups in the house and thereby evolve a bill of rights which would be acceptable to all, and one which would carry into effect the highest principles of citizenship.
I think I can safely say that in the course of the discussion on the amendment there was almost unanimity, as close an approach to it as can ever be expected in a representative institution, on the need of a bill of rights. One hon. member after another rose in his place in the house in support of the principles embodied in the amendment which I introduced. Some hon. members took the stand that it was too much circumscribed, and that in any event it could not possibly be comprised in the few words which I used in the amendment. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if I could have order. I cannot compete with what goes on behind the curtains.
I was saying that there was general unanimity on the need of a bill of rights, but there was also fairly strong opinion expressed by the hon. members immediately to my left, by hon. members of the Social Credit party and others, that a bill of rights, to be effective, must comprise more than what was confined within the ambit of my amendment. Finally the government, represented by the president of the privy council, placed this view before the house. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) dealt with the whole question of rights, freedoms and privileges. As reported at page 1477 of Hansard he said:
The hon. member for Lake Centre and I are very close together in this thing, but I suggest to him to-night that this is far greater than this trivial and piffling amendment dealing with three simple rights among a multitude of rights . . .
Why cannot we in this parliament get together on this issue? Why cannot all parties form a committee to consider these things apart altogether from this bill? If necessary that committee could call in advisers from the various provinces.
Mr. Diefenbaker:	Is that not what I suggested?
Mr. Mackenzie:	It is not what this piffling
amendment says at all, and that is why I say we cannot support the amendment.
The minister joined with me and said there was very little difference between us. Apparently the only point of divergence was as to the method of operation. I can say that there was never any disagreement between us because I said the same thing as he said in my opening paragraph when I introduced the amendment. I suggest, therefore, that, being in entire agreement with my hon. friend and with those who have expressed themselves on this question-the leader of the C.C.F. party, the leader of the Social Credit party and others-now is the time for us to make a declaration that a bill of rights shall be brought into this parliament which will assure that what we all desire in this regard shall be now determined and declared.
Section 27 of the bill as passed reads as follows:
A Canadian citizen other than a natural-born Canadian citizen shall, subject to the provisions of this act, be entitled to all rights, powers and privileges and be subject to all obligations, duties and liabilities to which a natural-born Canadian citizen is entitled or subject and. on and after becoming a Canadian citizen, shall, subject to the provisions of this act-, have a like status to that of a natural-born Canadian citizen.
There were those who raised the objection that the amendment did not go far enough; that it did not comprise citizenship of those who were Canadians by birth. I believe it was the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) who raised that point, and it was an effective one. I could not but fail to accept it, because after all, what we are trying to do here is to get a bill of rights which will be the epitome of the wishes of all hon. members of the house. The section says:
... a Canadian citizen, shall, subject to the provisions of this act, have a like status to that of a natural-born Canadian citizen.
I know of no other section which would permit of a definition of the rights of citizenship. Having regard to the measure of agreement that there is amongst us, and answering the appeal made by the minister in which he asked us all to get together, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon):
That the said bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend it as follows:
Canadian Citizenship

1. By adding subsection 2 to section 27 as follows:
"27 (2) That when this act comes into force, if parliament be then sitting or if parliament be not then sitting within ten days after the next session begins, the question of adopting a bill of rights, so as to assure the maintenance and preservation of democratic and traditional processes of liberty and of equality under the law of all Canadian citizens without regard to race, creed or colour, shall be submitted to the House of Commons in a resolution to be considered in a select committee properly representative of the entire population of Canada."
Sir, by this amendment the views of all hon. members on all sides of the house will have an opportunity for expression. Out of that common expression and common cooperation -because after all this matter is above partisan consideration-there will come a declaration that will assure the preservation of democratic rights and ensure that in the years to come men and women, Canadians all, will be able to look back and say: These are our rights; no longer are they nebulous; no longer do they consist only in tradition and in precedent. They have been epitomized by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I do not at this time propose to discuss the merits or demerits of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I desire only to refer Your Honour to the obvious rules of the house. In doing so I would refer Your Honour to paragraph 710 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, at page 238. I quote:
All amendments which may be moved on a second reading of a bill may be moved on the third reading with the restriction that they cannot deal with any matter which is not contained in the bill.
That is taken from May at page 421. Then, again, quoting paragraph 712 in the same volume:
On the third reading of a 'bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act-
Most of us were in the house at that time. -an amendment was moved that the bill be not now read a third time because it does not provide for complete government ownership of the Bank of Canada. This amendment involved the main subject matter dealt with in the bill. The Speaker ruled it out of order on the ground that it was an expanded negative.
And thirdly, at paragraph 713 in the same volume:
On the motion for the third reading of a bill to incorporate the Bank of Canada, an amendment that the bill be referred back to the committee of the whole, with instruction that they have power to amend same so is to safeguard the sovereignty of parlianieut over Canada's

financial policy, was ruled out of order for the following reasons:	"The amendment is irrelevant."
I submit that this amendment is irrelevant to any of the essential principles of the bill. The paragraph continues:
"The sovereignty of parliament cannot be affected by the passage of a bill in this house. The sovereignty of parliament is created and defined by the British North America Act, Section 91 of which states that it shall be lawful for the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to all matters, except those assigned to provincial legislatures and, inter alia, subjects enumerated therein, including banking, incorporation of banks and the issue of paper money. The sovereignty of parliament can only be affected by an amendment to the British North America Act."
This is the most decisive citation, where a Speaker's decision is approved by the House of Commons. It was moved that the bill be not now read a third time but that all the words after "that" be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
"The bill be referred back to the committee of the whole with the request-
Note those words, "with the request."
-that the government consider ways and means of providing compensation-
And so on. Then it continues:
Mr. Speaker ruled the proposed amendment out of order on the ground that a bill may be referred back with instruction either that the committee have power to amend it in certain particulars or for further consideration; it cannot be referred back-
These are the words upon which I base my contention-
It cannot be referred back with the request that certain matters be considered by the government.
That was a decision of a Speaker, upheld by the House of Commons. The same principle is now involved in the amendment now offered by the hon. member.
Again at page 503 of the same volume:
On the motion for third reading: (a) Amendment proposing to refer a bill back to the committee of the whole -with instruction to amend it so as to safeguard the sovereignty of parliament is out of order.
As I said before, speaking with the consent of such of my colleagues as were present, I made certain declarations the other evening. The hon. member for Lake Centre is now endeavouring to anticipate, by way of direction, the policy of the administration and government of Canada by forcing it into a position where it does not belong. I suggest that the hon. member's amendment is entirely out of order.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it appears to me that an examination of the precedents put before Your Honour by the leader of the house will show that they are not analogous to this situation. It would appear to me that an amendment to the motion for third reading is in the same category as an amendment to second reading, provided it does not introduce a new subject. That makes this amendment clearly in order, because it introduces no new subject. Section 27 of the bill deals with the rights and obligations of Canadian citizens. The proposition is not that any direction should be given to the government of the day with regard to what it should do or what it should not do, but rather that an opportunity be given parliament and the House of Commons to discuss the reason why, in the opinion of so many people, it is necessary that a bill of rights be considered by parliament.
I suggest that the amendment by no means introduces a new matter of business; it does not bring in any new subject. It deals with a subject already dealt with in section 27 of the bill. For these reasons I suggest the amendment is in order.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I have a word on the point of order? I am referring to standing order 77, and citations 813 and following. That paragraph or citation states:
When a bill comes up for third reading a member may move that it be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it in any particular.
It seems to me that the house always has authority to govern its own procedure. The fact that rulings of Speakers in different parliaments from time to time have been upheld by those parliaments should not bind subsequent parliaments for ever. We now have before us an amendment to the third reading of the bill which purports to give to the house what most hon. members desired when the bill was in committee. It seems to me that, despite the rulings of former Speakers, upheld by former parliaments, this is a new parliament, and as such it has the right to make decisions as to its own rules and their interpretation. We should not be for ever bound by decisions made in the past.

No; I am saying it. It was discovered that more than forty nations adhered to the rule set forth in section 13 of our Naturalization Act as amended in 1931, in consequence of the Hague conference, and that only five countries, the most signal and outstanding of which was, of course, the United States of America, had departed from it. The other countries were Paraguay, Uruguay, Russia, and Guatemala. So the whole world, with the exception of these five countries-and with great respect to them all, I suppose we are more interested in what was done in the United States than in what was done elsewhere-follows the rule which we are abandoning.
The United States abandoned the rule for an economic reason. A number of her citizens were leaving the United States, taking up their domicile in some sunny isle of the Pacific, or even coming to Canada, where, in those days, taxes were lower than they were in the United States. In this way they were escaping some of the burdens of citizenship while at the same time enjoying all the benefits thereof. That was the reason for the change in the United States legislation.
I am going to read into the record our present law, as enacted in 1931. This amendment to the Naturalization Act was enacted to meet a very difficult situation which came about after the United States had abandoned the rule of domicile and accepted that of nationality. It happened that in the course of the last war some Canadian women married citizens of the United States. The result was that these women were not citizens of the United States because by the legislation of that country they were denied citizenship. They ceased to be British subjects in Canada, because, according to our law, they had forsworn their allegiance, or had lost their nationality by marrying citizens of the United States. One very painful case, with which a number of members in 1931 were fully familiar, came to the attention of the house. A young Canadian woman married a citizen of the United States, and a child was born. He was not in enjoyment of perfect health. The woman could not get a Canadian passport because she was not a British subject in

Canadian Citizenship
Canada. She could not get a United States passport because she was not a citizen of that country. She could not cross the boundary line because she had this child, who was infirm, and who was not wanted here or there.
This hardship occasioned the amendment of 1931. That amendment to section 13 of the Naturalization Act is as follows:
13. (1) The wife of a British subject shall be deemed to be a British subject, and the wife of an alien shall be deemed to be an alien, except as in this section otherwise provided.
(2)	Where a woman who is a British subject marries an alien she shall not by reason only of her marriage cease to be a British subject unless by reason of her marriage she acquires the nationality of her husband.
(3)	Where a man, during the continuance of his marriage, ceases to be a British subject, his wife shall not cease to be a British subject unless by reason of the acquisition by her husband of a new nationality she also acquires that nationality.
(4)	Where notwithstanding the provisions of the last foregoing subsection a married woman would cease to be a British subject, it shall nevertheless be lawful for her within six months after the date at which she would cease to be a British subject, or in special circumstances with the consent of the minister within any longer period than six months, to make a declaration that she desires to retain British nationality, and thereupon she shall be deemed to have remained a British subject.
(5)	Where a certificate of naturalization is granted to an alien his wife, if not already a British subject, shall not be deemed to be a British subject unless within six months after the date of that certificate, or in special circumstances with the consent of the minister within any longer period than six months, she makes a declaration that she desires to acquire British nationality and upon the making of such declaration she shall be deemed to be a British subject.
(6)	Where an alien is a subject of a state at war with His Majesty it shall be lawful for his wife, if she was at birth a British subject, to make a declaration that she desires to resume British nationality, and thereupon the minister, if he is _ satisfied that it is desirable that she be permitted to do so, may grant her a certificate of naturalization.

That is an exceptional case. I am not certain that the law can meet all cases which arise. But it seems to me that a short paragraph added to section 13, which I have read, would meet the case mentioned by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
However, we are only talking about marriage between a citizen and an alien. No one suggests that marriage is always what we are pleased to call successful. Even between natural-born citizens, marriages fail. I assume that so long as humanity is what it is, there will be people united in marriage who are not happy and do not agree. But I submit that we should endeavour to eliminate as many of the causes of disagreement as possible, and I suggest that dual nationality in the home is not getting the young people off to as good a start as they are entitled to. If it be objected that the young woman should not be obliged to accept the nationality of her husband, I would say that if she elected to maintain her own nationality, she should have the privilege of doing so; the act could be amended in consequence. What seems to me wrong is that the alien wife should be denied that right at the present time and forced to remain an alien for a period, even for one year. Marriage brings about changes. It changes the status of the woman, it changes the name of the woman, it changes the domicile of the woman, and it changes likewise frequently the domicile and responsibilities of the man. It is a new status, and it requires a surrender of certain rights and prerogatives which pertain to what is called single blessedness.
I come to another aspect of the case which seemed to arouse a little scorn the other day; I refer to the financial or the economical aspect of it. If the woman retains her nationality of origin, she remains subject to the laws of her own country. In the United States the rule of domicile has been abandoned for the rule of nationality, and a person pays income tax, and his estate or succession pays inheritance tax, or succession duty, if he be a national, regardless of where he is domiciled. So if a lady from the United States marries a Canadian and retains her nationality, her property at death is subject to inheritance tax in the United States regardless of where it is situated, and is likewise taxable in Canada because she was domiciled here. If she is domiciled in Canada the succession duty acts of the dominion and of the several provinces will apply to her estate. It may be possible to revamp our legislation to meet this change in the citizenship bill, but the whole British scheme of polity and
Canadian Citizenship

international policy accepts domicile as the determining factor for taxation. This act is a departure from the rule which has obtained and still obtains in British countries, and is bringing in a new rule which, I submit, will cause confusion, and in some cases hardship, and possibly loss of property. I do not consider that there has been any sufficient reason set forth to depart from the age-old rule that obtains in the dominion and in the different provinces, that obtains in Canada in its relations with the British isles and other entities in the British commonwealth of nations. I do not think that any reason has been advanced sufficient to warrant the scrapping of that age-old and equitable rule.
If a woman feels that her rights have been invaded by the fact that she has by law become a British subject by reason of her marriage to a British subject, or ceased to be one by reason of her marriage to an alien, I should not be greatly opposed to a measure which would enable her to elect at the time of marriage whether she desired to retain her nationality or accept that of her husband. I think it is the very rare case where the woman deciding to'many is not desirous, is not hopeful, that utmost unity will prevail in the family and in the home about to be established. I was delayed for weeks and weeks while my husband procured ar certificate; but had he not gone to this trouble, and had his father not taken out his citizenship I might have found myself in the position in which thousands of other Canadian women have found themselves, of having inadvertently lost citizenship and become aliens.
Having been a candidate for office on three occasions; having done poll work several times and helped to make up voters' lists, I know of dozens and dozens of girls who have come of age and have found that without their knowledge-because they knew nothing of law; they only got married-they were suddenly no longer Canadian citizens but aliens, and unable to vote. I am sure the hon. member for Stanstead would not wish to perpetuate that condition. Undoubtedly all hon. members who believe in the rights of human beings-not the rights of men and women as opposing factions, or as two groups which have nothing to gain or lose, but as human beings-will want to see people have certain inalienable rights. Citizenship should be one of those rights.
In the long process of history, in the long march of civilization, we have gradually struck from women those shackles. We started out with woman as the property of man. It is not many years since a man could will his unborn child away from the mother. It is not many years since a woman did not have. the right to own property in her own name, after marriage. Automatically it went to the husband.
These are forward steps we have taken, writing into the statutes of our country the rights of human beings, regardless of their being men or women. I should like to congratulate the minister-and I should have done it much earlier-upon the stand he has taken.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
I wanted to call item 26 for the purpose of answering a question which was asked yesterday and putting in order any discussion with regard to it. This explains my absence from the chamber for the last hour or so. It concerns subsidies for dairy products. The position which has been taken by the government in relation to the matter results in an announcement of policy which concerns milk products over a period of time. I am not in a position at the moment to cover all the milk products, but those which have been most under discussion in recent days I am in a position to deal with.
In the first place, it has been decided that the consumer subsidy on fluid milk will be removed as of June 1, and control over prices will be returned from that date to the pro-
Supply-Agriculture

vincial milk boards. That is, in so far as control of prices is concerned the position will revert to where it was prior to the coming into effect of the prices board so far as fluid milk prices are concerned. In order to allow provincial boards an adequate period in which to make necessary price adjustments, a subsidy of fifty-five cents per 100 pounds will be paid to producers of fluid milk from May 1 to September 30, 1946, it being understood that this subsidy will be removed completely at the later date. It is provided that the subsidy be limited to thirty-five cents in areas where the agricultural food board considers this adequate. That is replacing the provision which was there before, that in those certain areas the limit was twenty-five cents. In view of recent adjustments in the price ceiling on butter, no further action in respect of the present subsidy on butter fat for creamery butter is considered to be required. It is necessary for certain reasons to give further consideration to the subsidies on milk entering into cheese, and into processed milk. The result of these discussions will be announced shortly, that is within the next few days. It is definitely understood that if any adjustments are made they will be upward as compared with the present summer subsidy. That is, if any adjustments are made on the cheese and the processed milk those adjustments will be upward as compared with the subsidies provided for the summer.
I have called the item "dairy products" under "marketing" in order to make it possible for hon. members, without being out of order, to ask any questions they desire to ask or to carry on any discussion in relation to it.
Availing myself of that suggestion, I will ask the minister if he will state whether there is any intention on the part of his department to increase the ceiling price of creamery butter.

I just made the
announcement in connection with butter, that action with regard to butter has already been taken. It is proportioned to the action which is being taken in connection with other milk products.
But the minister stated the other day that, in spite of the action taken, there is still a discrepancy in the return to the producer who makes butter instead of cheese; he does not get as much money.

I was really arguing that if there was a change over from cheese to butter, as apparently there had been in the province of Quebec, where it was easier for them to do it, where they have gone up very much in butter production, the indications
{Mr. Gardiner.J
were that there was something in favour of butter production. That is simply because of the taking off of the small subsidy which had been paid by the Quebec government, they switch over from cheese to butter, which would indicate that if there is any difference anywhere else it is a very small one.

speechtext: The consumer milk subsidy comes off from the first of June.

Some days ago the minister in answer to questions asked by various hon. members stated that when the subsidies on agricultural products were removed the Farm Prices Support Act would be brought into action and that the floor prices under the various agricultural products would be announced. Already there have been several removals of subsidies on agricultural products, on canning vegetables, canning fruit, and now on milk. I would ask the minister when it is intended to bring into operation the Farm Prices Support Act and place floor prices on these particular products. We are having shortages to-day of most agricultural products, and in my opinion one of the reasons for those shortages is the present uncertainty with regard to prices. I am quite sure that is one of the main reasons for the drop in production in quite a few lines. As regards dairy products, we find that figures were placed before the house showing a great increase in the export of dairy cattle at the present time, and one of the main reasons is that there is no certainty as to what prices for dairy products will be in the near future. I would like the minister, if he can, to inform us when floor prices will be placed under these products under the authority of the Farm Prices Support Act, which was passed by this house just before the last election.

The Farm Prices "Floor" Act, as it has been described-and that is as good a term to describe it as any, I think- was put on the statute books at the last session prior to the election, and when that bill was before the house the statement made was to the effect that the bill would be brought into operation at any time it was necessary to. bring it in for the purpose of maintaining returns to farmers. Returns include both price

Supply-Agriculture
and subsidy. Under the discussions we had at that time I think both terms were included. It would be brought into effect at any time it was necessary to retain the returns to farmers in a position which would be comparable with that of the last three years prior to that time. What was had in mind at the time was this, that farmers had been receiving for their products certain returns which were considered to be fairly reasonable in relation to the prices they had to pay for what they had to buy.
Quite an effort was made to have us say that those prices would be based on parity. We did not say that in those terms, because there are so many different interpretations of the word "parity" that it would be most difficult to justify ourselves one way or the other. But we did say that the relationship between what the farmers were getting and what they were paying would be taken into consideration when a decision was being reached as to when we would put the bill into effect.
The present position is that the bill has already been declared operative, and there is an item of $50,000 in these estimates for its administration. The new membership has not yet been appointed. At the time the bill was going through I stated that we would appoint a permanent chairman and that two officials of the Department of Agriculture would act as temporary members of the commission to function until such time as it might become necessary for the board to operate to control any downward trend in the prices of farm products. I do not think it would be correct to say that there has been any downward trend in the returns received by the farmers up to 'the moment, when you take into consideration both prices and subsidy, so that there has been no reason up to the moment for taking any action beyond what has been taken, as a result of anything that was said at the time the bill was going through.
The present position is not exactly as stated by the hon. member for Melfort. There is not a shortage in Canada in the production of farm products. There is, of course, a shortage in satisfying all the markets of the world, because there is a gfeater demand from other countries for Canadian farm products than we are able to supply. But the shortage is not in Canada. There is no shortage of food for Canadian consumption except in butter, and every year since I have had to do with public affairs, there has been a shortage of butter to supply the needs of the Canadian people. But so far as all other farm products are concerned there is a surplus supply, as I recall at the moment, with the possible exception of feed grain, and that is
because everything else is so high. We have not the feed grains at present to make absolutely certain that we can feed all the live stock we have through until we have a new crop, and unless the promise of crop conditions changes materially within the next month we are not going to be concerned so much about finding markets for our farm products as we shall be concerned about feeding the live stock we have. I have been suggesting for over a year that what we need to be most concerned about in this country is getting feed. We have never been in such danger of not having enough feed as we are right now. One of the reasons for that is that we have met in greater degree I think than any other country all the demands that are being made upon us for grain to feed the different peoples of the world to keep them alive. We have been going far beyond anything we are justified in doing in order to provide for them. That is the only shortage we are likely to have in the immediate future in the production of farm products. Any other shortages we may have will depend upon the feed supply.
The position then is that we have been maintaining prices at the levels at least at which they were before, and we have been increasing them from time to time.
So far as this particular product is concerned, we are now simply saying that, we are turning the control over prices and distribution back to where it was before, to the provincial boards which were handling it until it was taken over by the prices board, and we shall not be in a position to say whether the floor prices bill should be applied in connection with the products until we see the results of the action that will be taken between now and September. During that period we are going to be paying higher subsidies than we ever paid before, and so far as we know the producer is going to be receiving higher prices than he received during the three years of which I spoke. We shall not be in a position to take any action under legislation or under anything that was said until we see the results of the action taken between now and September.

Is the minister
going to press for the passing of this item to-day?
I will ask to have it stand after we get through with this discussion.

I should like to read a letter that I received to-day from a farmer in my constituency dealing directly with the statement just made by the minister with respect to feed and the reason for the reduction in production. This man's letter has to do with bacon.
Probably I have the same letter.

This man's letter is dated May 11, 1946. He says:	*
Dear Sir:
Some time ago I saw in the Star-Phoenix an article giving Mr. Gardiner great praise for giving the farmers two dollars more for their hogs. Well, ten days ago I took out my first load of winter hogs, and what did I get? Six Bl's 'and one C-something I never got in all the hogs I have sold before, and I have sold in the last six years an average of from 160 to 200 hogs per year.
The packers cannot tell me that I do not know an A hog when I see one. We have the best boar that money can buy and we have nine sows farrowed at the present time. We have 100 living pigs out of 114. We don't always have that luck.
Mr. Gardiner makes us farmers laugh when he says that it is the shortage of feed that has made the farmer quit raising hogs. There is plenty of feed. Give the farmer the price and he will give you the hogs and plenty of them. We have 22 brood sows that we intended to breed, to come in in November, but unless we are guaranteed $32 a hog we are out for good and my neighbours likewise. I am sending you my returns and I want you to let Mr. Gardiner and Mr. King see them for themselves, if you can make out this scribbling and read "little Jimmie" this letter, as he has fooled us long enough. Please excuse mistakes as I have a crippled hand.
That is the attitude of the farmers, certainly in the northern part of Saskatchewan.

But that does not say that it is correct.
(Mr. Gardiner.]

That certainly is the
opinion in that part of the country, which is one of the biggest hig producing areas in the Dominion of Canada.

I do not know whether it is the same letter that was written to me, but very much the same facts were set out in a letter that was sent to me and which started out by asking me if I had had any better luck than this farmer had. I told him my own luck in connection with a shipment at that very time. I sent ten hogs to market and I just got the returns in the mail the day before this man's letter came. Of my ten hogs, I got all A and B except two, and I was sorry that I got A and B hogs, for the other two were heavy and I got more for them than I did for the A's and B's. There has been a lot of complaining about people not being allowed to produce heavy hogs. The change that has been made in the premium permits one to do without the premium of $2 on A hogs or $1 on B hogs and to receive $32 apiece for the heavy hogs. That is what I got. I got an average of $29 for A's and B's. I got the average, which this gentleman wants on heavies, of $32. So that sometimes these chaps who do all this figuring do not figure far enough. My hogs were all of one litter, all fed in the same pen, all having the same feed and the same care, and the heavy hogs brought me $32, while the A's and B's did not bring that much. All sorts of considerations have to be taken cognizance of in the individual selling of hogs.

I understood the minister to say this afternoon that the consumer subsidy of two cents a quart would be taken off milk on June 1.
That is correct.
And that the subsidy of fifty-five cents on whole milk would be continued until September 30.
That is correct.
Does that include all milk or just whole milk?
That is all milk delivered as fluid milk.

And there is no further action to be taken on butter?

.Mr. GARDINER: I should say that the fifty-five cents is in most of the areas as it is now under the present subsidy provisions; but there is a provision at present which says that there are certain areas in which it will not be above twenty-five cents. We are saying here that there are certain areas in which it will not be above thirty-five cents.
I understand there is no further action to be taken on butter but that so far as cheese and processed milk are concerned there is to be a further statement.
That is correct.
The minister said this afternoon that there has been no decrease in the production of any article except butter.
No, I did not say that. I said there was no shortage. The hon. member said there was a shortage of all these porducts in Canada. I said there was not a shortage.
There has been a decrease in the production of several articles?
Yes; that is correct.
The minister did say that so far as our domestic requirements are concerned there was no scarcity except in butter. Is that true?
Yes.

It may be true that there is no scarcity so far as our domestic requirements are concerned, but surely this country has to live up to the commitments we made last spring to the United Kingdom. Surely this government is not considering only our domestic requirements at a time when there is the greatest food shortage the world has ever known. Surely we are planning to feed the United Kingdom and the world in general during a period of near famine. The minister said this afternoon that he had made more on his two heavy hogs than he had made on his grades A and B.
I have the statement in my pocket to-night.
That was the statement the minister made this afternoon. Was that per 100 pounds or per hog?
Per hog.

If that be true, I suggest that the whole balance of our hog grading system that we have worked for twenty-five years to get can be upset in three months. We have worked to try to keep the Untied Kingdom market for hogs. If the minister's
statement be true, I suggest that some change should be made, either the dollar bonus that was taken off be put back on or-

May I suggest that I should not have made the reply I did this afternoon on this item at all. We are not on the item dealing with hogs. I called this item for the purpose of discussing the subsidies on milk. We shall have ample opportunity at a later date to discuss hogs. We got off the track for a moment, and I hope others will not follow that practice.
The minister made the statement.
Do not make me make another one.

We shall forget about hogs for the moment. The Agricultural Prices Support Act was passed in 1944. Is it the intention of this government to put that act into force this fall when the subsidies are taken off milk? I should like the minister to make a statement regarding that.

I made a statement with regard to that before recess. The statement is that it will not be put into effect, and there is no reason for putting it into effect in connection with any farm product until that farm product threatens to drop below the returns which farmers were receiving in the three years preceding the session during which the act was passed.

Are the farmers to be placed in the same position as they were in 1941 when ^ceiling prices. were frozen at a lower standard? Are prices to be allowed to drop below present prices and then a price floor put on at that lower price?
Three years prior to 1945 do not bring you back to 1941.
With regard to these subsidies coming off on June 1 or September 30, does the price ceiling on whole milk still apply, or is the ceiling eliminated too? Do producers sell on the open market then?
The ceiling is then set as it was before. The price at which milk is marketed is set by the milk boards in the provinces.
I wish to touch on the statement made by the minister this afternoon. Has the wartime prices and trade board washed its hands of the milk business?

The wartime prices and trade board will be through setting prices of milk immediately the provincial milk boards take over.
Supply-Agriculture
That is September 30.
That is on June 1.
The minister said that the subsidy of fifty-five cents per 100 pounds would remain until September 30.

Yes; the reason for that is that the prices board had the intention, ever since they took over, of eventually turning control over the marketing of milk back to the provincial milk boards that were set up for that purpose. In any discussions that have taken place they have always given the undertaking that they would try to turn it back as they took it over; that is, they would not leave the boards in the position where in twenty-four hours they hand them back the problems that have been created and ask them to take over from there and try to fix things up. What they are doing is saying to the boards: "You start to operate on June 1. We are taking off the consumer subsidy, but we are going to continue the producer subsidy until September 30." We are saying this through the Department of Agriculture, but the two have been working in cooperation all the time! We said, "We are going to continue the producer subsidy until September 30." That gives four months from June 1 to September 30, with the producer subsidy being paid, for the milk boards, producers and consumers in the provinces to adjust themselves to the new condition and control.
What will that subsidy be?
It will be fifty-five cents, the same as it has been throughout the winter. It dates back to May 1 and continues right through; payments are made right through on the basis of fifty-five cents.

I am annoyed about this two cent consumer subsidy coming off, because when you take that away you immediately strike at the women and children. There are many other subsidies we would be far better able to remove than the consumer subsidy on milk. Milk is the cheapest balanced food in the world to-day, and by doing this you are going to deprive a great many needy families of milk.
They can drink less pop.
I may tell the hon. member for New Westminster, who says they should drink less milk, that we want them to drink more milk than ever.
I said they should drink less pop, less Coca-Cola and things like that.

Well, I don't know; I never drink pop myself. I was never more serious

in my life than I am about this milk situation as it affects the children of Canada today. The government knows what resulted from our children being undernourished in the thirties; when we needed those boys to fight a war for us we found they were not physically fit, largely because they had not had sufficient milk to drink. We have had girls going to school in the larger cities of Canada and fainting, and doctors have said that if they had plenty of milk to drink that would not happen. In my opinion the government is making a mistake in taking the consumer subsidy off milk to-day. The consumer should be the last person to be interferred with where milk is concerned. I do not know what influence the Minister of Agriculture has with this cabinet, but I believe this matter should be reconsidered before June 1. The minister will remember I used to tell him how to go about grading hogs, that it should be done gradually, and that is the way this thing should have been done. Instead of that the government takes away the whole thing at one time and does not let people become accustomed to paying one cent a quart more. All at once they will have to pay two cents more, and I do not think that is right.

We are all equally concerned in regard to children getting milk, but the position is hardly as it has been described. The first request for the removal of the subsidy came from the dairy branch of the Canadian federation of agriculture. That was two years ago, I think, or a year ago at the very least.

Was that the consumer
subsidy ?

Yes. The suggestion was made this spring by similar sources that we have been too long in doing this, that the only time you can take off a consumer subsidy is in the flush season of milk production. It was suggested, in the discussions which have taken place with regard to this matter, that we should have taken it off earlier, the reason being that it should not be necessary in the flush season to charge the whole two cents up to the consumer. Of course in increasing the producer subsidy on milk it is a fact that this subsidy does take care of the returns of the producers, which will make it possible for milk boards in the provinces to consider whether or not, at any time within the next five or six months, they should consider in any event putting the whole cost of the removal of the consumer subsidy on the consumers of milk. Those are all facts which were in the minds of persons who had to consider when this ought to be

Supply-Agriculture
done, if it ever should be done, whether it should be done in the fall of the year or in the spring. On balance it was finally agreed that the best time to do it, if it were to be done, was in the flush season of milk production, the season we are going through now. So from that point of view the decision was made to announce the removal of the con=umer subsidy at the same time as we *announced the increased producer subsidy being allowed on whole milk, giving four months in which to adjust the situation to meet whatever conditions prevail next fall.

I am sorry it has been found necessary to remove the subsidy on milk supplied to consumers. I agree with the hon. member for Selkirk that the more milk we can encourage our people to use, the healthier they are likely to be. Of course if this were being done in order to restrict the use of milk so that we might assist those in the areas of starvation the matter might be looked at a little differently.
What I really rose to say was that I was a little surprised at a statement made by the minister this afternoon, which I wrote down as he said it, in connection with the supplies that we are sending overseas and what we are doing in connection with the feeding of the starving world. He said: "We are going far beyond anything we were justified in doing."
I meant with regard to grain only.
That was not clear in my mind, and I thought it would be a pity if that were interpreted elsewhere as I interpreted it-	.
Feed stuffs particularly for live stock.

-because, while I would like to commend the government for what the government and the country have done in regard to meeting the needs of the starving people of the world, my opinion is that we could do more than we are doing to give that relief at the present time. I do not want to say anything that seems a bit invidious, though it may be; but in comparison with the disappointing record of our great neighbour to the south I think we have done well, though I do not believe we have done nearly all we might. I notice that in the newspapers to-day, as I noticed a few days ago, we were told that Great Britain out of her meagre supplies is going to allot some 200,000 tons of food more to the starvation zones of Europe and in order to assist as far as possible in the relief of a threatened famine of huge dimensions in India.
Most of which will be wheat she got from Canada.

That is quite true. But I have been greatly surprised to read a suggestion in the newspapers by a prominent United States citizen who has been across the world that Great Britain should relinquish her supplies in order to assist, the inference being that these small reserves will be useful in order to meet the needs of the world. While I do not know just what the position is regarding reserves in Canada, I would say this immediately: that having been twice overseas during the war, and receiving frequent letters from friends and relatives across the seas, I believe the condition over there is worse now than it was at any time during the war, and I can well understand why a few reserves should be kept on that island. We must realize that every ounce of food that is imported has to be brought in by ship, and that in the event of a drastic coal strike in the United States, or anything else that would interfere with the shipping of food from this side of the Atlantic, with no reserves they, too, would be faced with starvation in a very short while. I think we should do everything we can to send every available ounce of food to the starving people of the world. We should say nothing and do nothing that would lend any colour to the idea that has gone abroad in some quarters that the United States is doing a very great deal, that we are doing a very great deal and that there are reserves across the seas which might be used to assist in the needs of the world.

Are not some of the difficulties confronting the people of Great Britain to-day, so far as food supplies are concerned, on account of the fact that a great proportion of their food is going to Germany?
That is right.
It is not actually on account of a lack of food.

I was saying that, that she is supplying starving countries. Undoubtedly one of those starving countries is Germany. We defeated Germany, and we have very little sympathy for those who brought a terrible holocaust upon the world. Yet, starvation in Germany would breed further difficulties, and ultimate revolt in Europe would react upon the rest of the world. Even if we had no other reason for doing all we can to feed the starving people of Germany, selfpreservation demands that we shall do so. While during the war we may have been pretty bitter against Germany, and might have suggested that she be made to suffer as she made the rest of the world suffer, nevertheless to-day we have to view the situation in a more realistic light, and realize that if certain events
Supply-Agriculture

happen in Germany, and particularly in that area of Germany which the British control, we are going to suffer for it.
I do not want to be out of order when discussing this item. But since the matter was raised by the minister in his statement this afternoon, at least in one part of it, I felt that one was entitled to say a few words on this point. After all, in our own country we are enjoying more than double the calories most of the people even in the fairly well fed parts of Europe are getting at the present time.
I believe the government could well urge the people to cut down a little more on what we are using, and to cut out some of our luxuries. I think we could do with a little less ice-cream, if necessary. And those who drink liquor could do with a little less malting barley than is going into liquor.
On a point of order, I do not wish to have to answer all these things.
I do not expect the minister to.

If I do we shall be discussing this question all night. I understood we were discussing an announcement made with respect to milk. It has been suggested that I raised these questions but I did not. They were raised by the hon. member for Melfort. I simply answered some of the things he said. If we are going into all those discussions, the whole of my estimates will be covered under this one item. I do not want to have to answer these things three or four times.
We are discussing milk subsidies, and I shall give all the information I can with regard to them. When that is finished we can go on to other agricultural estimates.

I shall be very glad to fall in line with the minister's suggestion. But I wish to say that I understood the minister-and I think if he will look at Hansard, he will realize it was a pretty bald statement-
The statement has entirely to do with feed grains.
It was not I thought confined in that way.
If the hon. member will read Hansard he will find it is.
We will both read Hansard.

Do we understand by the minister's statement regarding consumer subsidies on milk that the farmers will be expected to reduce the price in order to take up those two cents, which will mean approxi-

mately eighty cents less for their milk this Bummer, after getting the 20-cent rise in subsidy, with the increased cost of production? I think all farmers in Canada realize that the consumer is an important person. We, of all persons, remember that fact. At the same time, with the increase of twenty cents in subsidy, and then asking them to take part of that two cents, it would mean sixty cents less for their milk.

What I am suggesting is that that decision will be made by another authority, and that is an authority which is much closer to my hon. friend's own home. In other words, it is the central authority in Toronto, which is set up to deal with milk. I am not going to anticipate what decision they will make. They have complete authority to make a decision, just as the prices board has had authority in the past. I presume they are going to pass upon the facts as they find them.
But the minister will agree that it will put the farmer in a very poor light with the consumer.
Not if you have a good board in Ontario-and I think you have.

Do I understand from the minister that he now says that the Ontario milk board-and I take it that that is what he is referring to-will have the right to set the consumer price on milk? They never have had that right before, have they?
Yes.
No, they never have had that right before. They have acted more or less as referees when distributors in certain centres have petitioned to set a price. They have acted in that capacity.
Yes.
But they have never had the right to set the consumer price for milk, and I doubt very much whether they have that right to-day.
They can be given it.

I am told they have not.
I should like to ask a question, following up what has been said by my colleague the hon. member for Brant. Is the farmer to be expected to reduce the price of milk to the distributor, or is the general public or the consumer to pay the same price per quart for milk as he is paying to-day.

If I remember correctly, the set-up we are talking about was put into effect by the government of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. Most people in Canada

Supply-Agriculture
thought he did a very good job in making possible the milk boards that they have in the provinces. This was done as a result of discussions which took place at that time, and the decision arrived at was that the authority rested with the provinces.
There w'as no authority with the federal government at all, in ordinary times. The authority was with the provinces, in dealing with matters of that kind. So they have set up boards in every province of Canada, with the exception, I believe, of British Columbia. In its last session British Columbia passed legislation setting up its board. The result is that every province in Canada has a board which has the right to exercise any authority given it by the provincial legislature with regard to the marketing of milk within the province. They have control over the marketing of milk, and they will make the decision on the question now raised. I shall have no authority to make it, and I am not going to say what will be done.

I think the minister is entirely wrong about the board set up by the Bennett government. If I remember correctly, the board then set up was the dominion marketing board, and I understand the court in England threw out that legislation. Does the minister say that the provincial commissioner has power to set prices for milk or dairy products interprovincially ?

There are nine departments, and I should not like to state to the committee, without any of the facts in front of me, just what authority each one has. But they have whatever authority was given them by the respective provincial governments.
I am speaking from memory-and the hon. member for Haldimand will correct me if I am wrong-but I still think what was done was done by the Bennett government. I remember the hon. member for Haldimand stating at the last session, during a discussion with respect to setting up another board, that it was determined at that time that in dealing with commodities such as milk, which are produced to a great extent in the same province in which they are consumed, the authority is with the provincial governments. As a result of that, you have nine different boards handling the marketing of milk, with any authority they have given to them by the provincial legislatures. All the regulating from June 1, on, will be turned back to those boards, from which much of the authority was taken by the prices board when it was set up in 1941.

I am sorry if I was not in the chamber when the minister made his announcement, but I cannot be in two places at once. I was attending a committee meeting and I am not twins. I may be speaking out of turn, not knowing exactly what the minister's announcement was, but it seems to me that there are one or two things we have to determine. I have listened to the discussion and I have yet to understand why this subsidy is now being done away with.
I should like to ask three questions. Is it because the minister wants the people of Canada to have more milk? Is it because he' wants the producers to get more for their milk? Is it because he wants the consumer to be able to buy more cheaply and consume more milk?
I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Selkirk and I believe he is on the right track. What are we considering in connection with this matter? Are we considering the good of the people of Canada with respect to these subsidies? The minister followed the hon. "member for Selkirk and said that they were very much concerned about the consumption of milk by the people. The minister, speaking for the government, said, "We are worrying about that." I am going to suggest that there is something else the government is concerned about, that is their treasury. I do not think lam wrong when I say that this announcement has as its background the financial policy into which the government have let their feet slip over the past years.
They struck out with a policy of family allowances, and that cost a lot of money. They have done other things along similar lines which also cost a lot of money. I am not arguing against family allowances, but there is a little suspicion in the back of my mind that they did that as a political move. What I am saying now is that they have to cut expenses somewhere and this looks to me like one of the first announcements in an expense cutting programme.
Another thing the government has to do is reduce taxation. You cannot continue to spend and reduce taxation and balance your budgets. It just does not add up. I think it was rather unique, even though it was not clever, for the Minister of Agriculture to rise this afternoon and call for a certain item in order that he might make this announcement. As a matter of fact, although we may appear to be discussing milk, what we are actually discussing is something that comes under the Department of Finance because it is a subsidy. The Department of Finance has found itself in a box, and
Supply-A griculture

I would add that the whole financial policy under which the government has been working for years is beginning to crack down. If the minister does not change that policy the government is going to crack down with it, or crack up.
Blow up.

Perhaps blow up. I am
saying something now that I believe to be true. Are we considering the people of Canada in this matter, or are we considering the interests of the treasury in order that the government may meet the demands of the people for a reduction in taxation and still carry on some of their huge expenditures? I should like that answered and perhaps I shall have to wait until the budget before it is answered. While it is the Minister of Agriculture who is taking on this matter, rightly the Minister of Finance should be doing it. I notice the Minister of Finance is in his seat taking note of all that is being said.
I shall close my remarks by saying that the only way a country can be prosperous, the only way the people of a country can be happy and contented is to have an expanding economy. You cannot have an expanding economy without spending lots of money. Personally I am in favour of subsidies because they mean .an expanding economy. I am in favour of anything that will put money into the pockets *of the people. But there is juggling being done in these days. That was the trouble with the dominion-provincial conference. That conference was a matter of juggling with taxation, seeking to pull this piece over here and push that piece out over there. It was a case of saying, "You take this and I will take that." We might as well face the facts. There is no use in trying to put money into people's pockets with one hand and trying to pull out the same amount with the other.
Take the pocket with you.
The hon. member for Battle River says, "Take the pocket with you."
And the pants too.
Yes, and the pants too.
Draw the line somewhere.

We have to draw the line somewhere. We can talk about the people of Europe; we can talk about other things, but I suggest that we are missing the mark when we talk about them. Those are incidental big problems, but I am suggesting that this is a problem which comes from the treasury and is being put to us in this way.

In answering what has just been said I would recall that only two days ago, I believe, the hon. member for Macleod added his voice to that of a number of other hon. members who were complaining because too many announcements were made on the orders of the day and on motions and could not be discussed. It was said that the ministers were getting into the habit of making statements on important matters at a time when no one could say anything about them. The only reason this announcement was made in this way was to give every one an opportunity to say something about it.
We were considering whether it should be made by two ministers or one, but then the proposal was made that the announcement should be made on a certain item in my estimates so that everyone could discuss the matter. If we are to be criticized one day for putting out statements on motions in order to get them out to the country and then criticized when we make a statement before the house in committee of supply in order that the subject matter may be fully discussed, then I should like to ask the hon. member for Macleod when we can bring them in. When are these announcements to be made? I think they have been made in the proper way. We have even given the hon. member for Macleod an opportunity to make his speech and show that he thinks differently to-day from what he did a few days ago.
As to the other matter, the ceiling price of milk across Canada is set at different levels at different places, depending on the district. That ceiling still remains. What has been done is to take off the two cents subsidy, which was paid in this way. In a city like Ottawa, for instance, if the ceiling price on milk is twelve cents the consumer pays ten cents, and the distributor of the milk collects two cents by way of subsidy, called consumers' subsidy, which makes it possible for him to deliver the milk at two cents less than the ceiling price in this community. When the distribution of the milk is handled by some other authority, they may or may not charge the consumer more. If they do not charge the consumer more, then on the principle that people will drink more milk when they can get it more cheaply, there will be just as much milk consumed under the new plan as under the old. If, on the other hand, they increase the price of milk to people living in a particular area, the authority to which they appeal is much closer to the situation than any authority which operates in Ottawa alone.
It is a further fact that conditions are not the same in the different provinces or in different parts of the same province. There

Supply-Agriculture
are areas where milk is sold at seven, eight or nine cents a quart, and other areas where it is sold at twelve or thirteen cents a quart, depending upon the community. All the facts in relation to these communities are best known to the boards appointed by the provinces to deal with these matters. While control has been put back under these boards, we are simply following out the policy tfhich was announced at the very beginning, namely, that these controls were put on under the War Measures Act without which we had no authority by any other statute or under the constitution to go into a province or into homes and do the things in war time which in ordinary times we could not constitutionally do.
We' were told very politely in the meetings that were held and which were referred to a few moments ago that there are some people in the dominion who do not intend that we should continue exercising that authority. If that is the case, we had better turn back the authority as peacefully as we can to where it belonged in the first place, and do so as soon as possible. That is one very good reason for doing what we are doing. It is not intended that the mere doing of this shall determine any one of the three questions that were asked by the hon. member for Macleod at the beginning of his remarks. We are simply trying to restore the peace-time relationship as between the federal government and the provinces. This is one of the matters that must be dealt with at some time, and it has been suggested that this is the proper time to do it. There has been no question in anyone's mind that it would have to be done eventually, and the only question that remains is whether now is the time to do it or whether we should wait for another six or twelve months. I presume that my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party, judging by their speeches, would say that we have waited six months too long.

I am one of those who think we have waited too long. A little while ago the Minister of Agriculture brought my name into the discussion when speaking of the milk boards in the different provinces. I happened to be chairman of the committee on agriculture during the Bennett administration. That committee made an investigation into the whole milk question and recommended that boards be set up in the provinces because the provinces had the right to set prices. I think those milk boards did a good job.
I was sorry to learn from the minister's remarks that there is still a ceiling on the price of milk delivered to the consumer. If that
ceiling remains I do not see that the milk boards in the provinces can do much good by setting a price on milk, because it will be governed entirely by the present ceiling price of milk. I hope that that restriction will be removed very shortly.
It is all very well to say that we are not going to pay a two-cent bonus on milk delivered to the consumer; but if the milk board is to be stymied, if the board is to be put in the position where it must govern the price it sets by the ceiling price on milk at the present time, it will not get very far. It seems to me that that upsets the whole argument advanced by the minister in regard to removing the subsidy on milk at the present time. Since the minister has gone at least part of the way in accepting the policy laid down by our party I think the time has come for him to go the whole way and remove the price ceiling. I have a good deal of sympathy for the minister, because I do not think he is altogether in sympathy with the policies of the wartime prices and trade board at this time. Perhaps he is, but I do not think so. He is enough of a farmer to know that farm prices should not be governed as they are now by price ceilings set by the wartime prices and trade board. I hope that he will be successful in his fight with the wartime prices and trade board and will succeed in having the price ceilings changed, or at least that they will not be set as they are to-day by the prices board.

Before there is any further discussion I think I should reply to the last remarks of the hon. member. The wartime prices and trade board was set up to do a job in connection with the control of prices. I am candid enough to say that any farmer, as has just been suggested by the hon. member for Haldimand, would look with some misgivings at the suggestion that there be ceilings put on prices.
They still do.

But if you look back over history, you will find, and you have only to take a drive through rural Ontario to prove it, that the better farm buildings were all built during war periods,. as you can see by the dates on them. Some were built in the Crimean war, some in the South African war, some in the first great war; and the only reason we did not build more during the last war is that we could not get the materials.

There was one built in my riding.
Supply-Agriculture

An occasional one may-have been built but we have not built as many as we would have liked to build. That proves that the only time that farmers were able to get better than the ordinary revenue out of farming was during a war period.
Not in this war.

That is just what I am coming to. The difficulties the farmers went through before this war were caused by the preparation for war in other parts of the world, which resulted in no markets for our products. Then we came into the war, and the reason why the farmer had misgivings and why I had misgivings was that the farmer was denied the right to get very much more for his eggs than he got, very much more for his hogs than he got, very much more for his beef than he got and, more recently, more for his wheat than he got. That was all done under a control policy in order to prevent inflation. What I said, what many others said, what the majority of the government said-or it would not have been done-and what the whole government agreed to finally after discussion was that, in view of the fact that the farmer's price was held down during the war for at least three years, for a number of years after the war, provision should be made that the return to the farmer-call it price or subsidy plus price or whatever you like-was not to be allowed to go down unreasonably. If you maintain that policy long enough, then you will balance the fact that prices otherwise would have gone down against the fact that you did not allow them to go up.
I was asked a few moments ago, "When are you going to bring the price floor bill into operation in connection with these dairy products?" I answer, just so soon as prices of dairy products begin to go down to the level or approaching the level at which those who are working on statistics every day, as they have been now ever since that bill was passed, indicate that we are approaching the point where the farmer is being asked to take less for his product than he should have taken. That, by the way, is the answer to the suggestion made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Macleod.
It is not purely a financial question, as the hon. gentleman suggested. The financial side of it, in relation to the farmer's problems, is taken care of by the floor prices act which was passed in the last session before the election. This committee can rely upon it that, when it becomes necessary to. apply the terms of that act, they will be applied, and it will cost just as much to apply them as it would to continue subsidies or anything else in order to give protection to the farmers.

The act provides $200 million with which to do that job, and we have not spent that much on this kind of thing in any of the years we are talking about. Therefore it is not a matter of the treasury trying to protect themselves. But when one hears an hon. member say that all we are concerned about is the treasury, the question presents itself: What is the treasury? T]ie treasury in that sense means the money we are taking out of the pockets of the Canadian people; and when an hon. member says that we are thinking in terms of taxes, of course we are. But they are taxes paid by every person in the country in some form or another, and anyone who tries to run away from that resonsibility should not be in this house. That is the main job the government has: in the first place, trying to determine to what extent the people can pay for the cost of running the government; at the same time trying to collect more heavily from those who are in a position to pay most, and then, by such measures as the family allowance, to redistribute those funds back, in some part at least, to the people who did the work in order to make the production of wealth possible. That in a few words is the policy in relation to the whole matter. It has been put into effect throughout the war; it is still being put into effect, and that is one of the reasons why we are still here-to put it into effect.
I do not think the farmers of Canada found fault with price controls during the time of the war. They were willing to do their share and they did it.
And a great deal more than their share.

They produced to the limit. They feel now, however, when the war is over-and the minister will agree with me in this-that the time has come when they should have some reward. They bore their fair share of the burdens of price controls during the war-perhaps more than their share-and now that the war is over, they feel, quite rightly, that they should get their, fair reward for what has happened in the meantime.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry if we are to get into a discussion, on this item, of the merits of price control. I hope we shall not do so, because there is another debate in the house in which that question can be discussed. I find it hard to sit here and listen to the doctrine I hear propounded, that is to say, that at such a time as this, when the inflationary pressures are so great as they are now, this is

Supply-Agriculture
the time .of all times to take the lid off. I find it impossible to sit here and listen to that sort of thing with composure.
I simply want to make clear one thing with regard to the consumer milk subsidy. The situation on June 1, will be that the maximum, the price ceiling, will be established; that is, two cents higher than the consumer is paying at the present time. That will be established by the wartime prices and trade board, but thereafter the matter of adjustment in prices will be in the hands of milk boards.
Prices to the producer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The prices charged for milk, yes.
Paid for milk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Paid for milk; it is the same thing. I do not think there is anything more I can say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Following what the
Minister of Finance has said, may I remind the committe of the rules which are in effect in committee, according to which all discussion should be relevant to the item under consideration. There has been considerable latitude so far this evening, but I suggest to the committee that future discussion be confined strictly to the item under consideration.

The criticism that has arisen since the announcement has been made by the Minister of Agriculture is something about which a few members on this side of the house have been warning the government for at least the past one or two years. I think I can speak with the support of the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruiekshank) in this assertion, that the subsidy of two cents to the consumer does not meet the views of the farmer in the Fraser Valley. That is a definite statement. The hon. member for Selkirk brought up the question of milk consumption. The hon. member for Fraser Valley and I are members of the Fraser valley milk producers' association and we found that when the price of milk went up one cent the consumption of milk fell. It did not fall because the people had no money with which to buy milk. Consumption did not fall because the price had been raised. There was a psychological factor operating in the minds of many people against paying extra money to farmers for a good product. To-night when the hon. member for Selkirk was speaking I mentioned Coca-Cola. There is something strange that I have observed. You can raise the price of soft drinks, cigarettes, candy bars and there is no attack from the public, no criticism. But try to raise the price of milk one cent and the
whole country is up in arms. One thing that is bothering me is this: What will happen when the subsidy comes off? I am not advocating that the ceiling price be taken off the price of milk at the present time, but I am wondering what the farmer is going to do when the subsidy comes off at the end of September, because it is well known that he cannot produce milk at the price he is receiving if the subsidy comes off.
One reason why our people are not going on the land is that it is far easier to work in the city than it is to milk cows. I speak as one of the few members of the committee who can milk cows.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I know whereof I speak. I should like to take on any hon. member if he is talking about a competition.
Go and get the cow.

I certainly am speaking with more authority as a farmer than many of the lawyers and others who speak on the subject. I know whereof I speak.
