When the subsidy is lifted we are wondering what is going to take place on the farms where farmers are endeavouring to produce milk under present conditions, and will have to accept less when that time comes.
Some mention has been made about our people drinking more milk. We shall have to educate the people and their children to drink more milk. What do we find with regard to the drinking of milk? If you go into a restaurant or cafeteria and look around you will find it is the grown-ups who are drinking more milk, not the children. The children are drinking soft drinks. I have been told that in the canteens of the three services more milk was drunk by the members of the services during the war than any other kind of liquid, and that is all to their credit. What we need is to educate the parents and their children to drink the finest food that God has given us.

I am not entirely clear yet on this price control situation. I asked the Minister of Agriculture a pointed question a few moments ago. I understood him to say that after the subsidies came off the wartime prices and trade board were entirely through with the control of milk prices. From that time on it was a matter for the provincial boards. What the Minister of Agriculture said since, and what the Minister of Finance said a few moments ago have confused me again. I wish this point cleared up. In the section of the country from which I come
Supply-Agriculture

many dairymen are supplying towns of one or two thousand population. When the order setting the ceiling price came into effect the prices that they were charging the inhabitants in the towns or cities were not all the same. The prices at which they were selling were the prices that existed when the freeze was put on. I want to know whether there is any further price control on the small dairy producers when the subsidies come off. Hitherto in my province they have received no direction whatever from the provincial dairy boards. Are they entirely clear of price ceilings so far as the wartime prices and trade board is concerned? From that date on can they set their own prices for their whole milk?

May I say one word regarding boards? I know something of the power of boards because I have had a good deal to do with them. I am now speaking of British Columbia and I suppose this applies to all the provinces. The provincial boards were given the power to control all matters absolutely so long as the articles for sale were sold within their provinces; but if the article, whether it be milk, fruit or potatoes, were exported to another country or province, then the regulations and power of the dominion applied. But so far as the provinces are concerned, these provincial boards have all the power they need. That is the information I have received.
Might I have an answer to my question? So far as the federal order is concerned, is it completely eliminated on that date?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I tried to make it clear before that on June 1, that is beginning with midnight on May 31, the consumer subsidy will be withdrawn, and the ceiling price, as it was before the consumer subsidy was paid, will be restored. That will be the situation on June 1. Now, then, that will be the way the period after June 1 starts off.
The price will be twelve cents?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In many markets, I think in Ottawa, the price to the consumer is now ten cents, and with the withdrawal of the subsidy the .ceiling will be twelve cents.
It varies in different districts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; it is different all over Canada.
Two cents above what the consumer is paying to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well-
No.
The subsidy is paid directly to the distributor. Will the ceiling be placed at two cents above what the consumer is paying?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is substantially correct, yes. I do not know whether it is 100 per cent correct, but it is substantially correct. The ceiling that was in existence before the consumer subsidy was instituted, which was in December, 1942, if I remember correctly, becomes the ceiling. There may have been some adjustments in some districts in the meantime. Substantially that old ceiling comes back.
I wish to point out, while I am on this subject, that this subsidy is the only one in existence that "has had the effect of depressing the price of a product to the consumer below the price that he was paying in the basic period, the fall of 1941, with the result that milk prices in Canada are remarkably low by any comparison that can be made, especially with milk prices in the United States. On leading markets there the prices are very much higher than they are in Canada. I say that in answer to the hon. member for Selkirk who is worrying about the fact that with the elimination of the subsidy the consumer will be obliged to pay more. That is so, but he will not be paying more than he was paying during the basic period, namely, the fall of 1941. That is substantially true from coast to coast. There may be a few exceptional communities where adjustments have been made, but that is substantially the case.
I wish to make this point clear: If the control of the price of milk is to be restored to the provincial authorities pursuant to a policy of gradual decontrol, then it follows that we cannot continue to pay a federal subsidy, because it would be sheer irresponsibility for the government to leave the fixing of the price to provincial authorities with freedom to them to put it up or down, and at the same time be pouring in federal money. If the federal government is to continue to pay a consumer subsidy on milk it must continue to control the prices, it must continue to be the authority which fixes the price.
That is Drew's argument in reverse.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want to get drawn into a cross-current like that.
Therefore, if we are right in decontrol, then we have to withdraw this consumer milk subsidy. I think we are right because, as time goes on, it becomes increasingly difficult for the federal authority to be fair in the adjustments which it makes. For example, a situation might arise in Saskatchewan which called

Supply-A g riculture
for an upward adjustment of the ceiling price. If the federal authority is the body that is fixing the price at which milk is sold that action is cited as a precedent in other provinces, and accusations are likely to be made that there is discrimination by the federal authority between one part of the country and another; whereas in a country such as this, conditions vary greatly, and in such a matter as the fixing of milk prices-I do not say everything, I may say to my hon. friend- surely it is more appropriate for the local boards to be fixing them than the federal authority. We should get to that position as soon as possible.
I also wish to say that this is a remarkably difficult subsidy to administer. I suppose hon. members realize that every month from twenty to twenty-five thousand cheques have to be sent to dealers and distributors in all parts of Canada; and without a large and competent staff, which the board finds it difficult to maintain, it is difficult to apply fully and satisfactorily the safeguards that ought to be applied to the expenditure of public money. There is no doubt about that; and the board is finding it increasingly difficult to keep a competent staff. Members of their staff are going back to their businesses and to the employment from which they came. This highly involved and complex consumer milk subsidy is the sort of thing that it is increasingly difficult to administer.
Those, I think, are the main points I wanted to cover. The hon. member for Souris asked me a question which I find it a little difficult to answer.
I find it difficult to understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is not difficult to understand, but the part of the question I am finding it difficult to answer is this. The hon. member says there was no control whatever exercised by the provincial milk boards in some parts of some provinces, and he wants to know' whether this policy involves removing' some sales completely from control. I cannot answer that.
As far as your authority is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot answer that.

You are keeping the ceiling on milk.
Mr, ILSLEY: We are restoring the 1941 ceiling on June 1, and then we propose to permit the price to be fixed and controlled by the local boards.
That is the producer price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I want to go ahead with this and get to the bottom of it. If I can answer it I will say so, but I do not think I can. The hon. member for Souris says there are some sales of milk in some parts of some provinces which w:ere never subject to the control of milk boards. I did not know that.
That is the case all over Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not know that, and I do not pretend to know everything about this question. I was given to understand that the milk boards in the provinces had authority to control the prices of all sales of milk, with the exception of British Columbia, which was setting up a board. I thought that was the practice that would be resumed.
Then in that case you would not interfere if the producers in those areas went out and increased their prices; that is, there would be no interference as far as your board is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a situation I would have to look into.
The milk boards will set those prices, surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought thej' would; I thought it was a matter which the milk boards in the provinces could and did control. If there is a situation, a real problem there of some sales not being under the control of anybody, then it is a matter I shall have to look into.

I think I can explain what the hon. member for Souris has in mind; at least I want to find out if it is what he has in mind. In the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan there is no milk control except in the cities.
That is it.

In Saskatchewan there is control in Regina, Saskatoon, Moose Jaw and Prince Albert, and there may be a little control in places like Battleford; but there is no control at all outside those cities. There has never been any control there; the board never attempted to go out and say what I should pay another farmer for milk, or even what the people in the smaller communities should pay.
Yes, they did.
They did within limits, but no one ever tried to enforce it seriously.

They did enforce it right in my constituency.
Supply-A griculture
When you get it back under the provincial boards you will not have much difficulty in that regard.
I should like to ask a simple luestion there. Did not the prices board set she price at which milk should be distributed in the cities? If they did not I am very much mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.

I do not know whether the Minister of Finance really heard what I said. I stated I was very much annoyed because this consumer subsidy was being removed all at once. I thought that was too drastic, and I do not see even yet why the two cents should be taken off all at once. The hon. member for New Westminster spoke about the subsidy decreasing the demand for fluid milk, but that has not been the experience in Manitoba. We are selling more milk in Winnipeg to-day than ever before. If I am not mistaken, one month's production was up about two and a half million pounds. Hon. members will find the exact figures at page 1387 of Hansard, when I spoke in the house previously. We do not want the children to drink pop if they will drink milk. I cannot seem to get hon. members to realize that. Now that we have created a market for milk, let us not lose that market because of the removal of this subsidy. The more the people have to spend, the more they will buy; and if you take off the subsidy you are destroying the farmers' sale for milk; you are endangering the health of the people, and there are other disadvantages. I hope the Minister of Finance will reconsider this matter. Do not take off the two cents at once. If you must reduce taxation, do it gradually, but do not pick on the workingman first. Let him come later on. You have given in to the pressure of big business and taken off the subsidies and ceilings on different things the workingman has to buy. Now you are attacking the food he has to purchase. Please do not do that.

On many occasions I have tried to point out to the house that the foundation on which our farm price structure has been erected in the past was entirely faulty. When the government brings into operation the good things that are supposed to be provided for us in the Agricultural Prices Support Act I hope some consideration will be given to the hours that are worked by farmers and their wives and families, and the prices they have to pay for the things they buy, before those prices are fixed. Perhaps hon. members will be surprised to learn that in July, 1942, we were receiving for our wheat an initial price of 17J cents a bushel less than we were receiv-

ing when this government came into office in 1935, just when we were beginning to get out of the depression. Many people do not realize this and manyother things in connection with agriculture. I should like to see the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce get busy and employ some real statisticians. I believe they now have such people in the government service, but under the policies adopted they are not allowed to do the work they should be doing in the interests of the farmers and, therefore, in the interests of all the people of Canada. So once again I am pleading that the price structure, as far as farm products are concerned, should be upon a sound foundation. Give the farmer the forty or forty-four hour week that you are giving to organized labour and all the rest of the people in the country, and when you have a prosperous agriculture you can look with confidence to a prosperous and united Canada; but you cannot have it otherwise.

May I suggest that we have had sufficient discussion on this item to provide all the information necessary in connection with it. We can come back to it and discuss it further when we take up dairy products, or if any further information is required now it might be asked for, and then this item might be allowed to stand so that we might go on to a consideration of the estimates.
If prices of dairy products go below the cost of production, who will set the floor prices; will it be the provincial milk board, or the federal board?

The intention expressed at the time the bill was brought down is that if the marketing of farm products under the system that prevails brings a price which is satisfactory, as related to the actions taken during the three years referred to, there will be no necessity for doing anything under the floor prices bill.
Just by way of illustration, let us take the product which to a certain extent will control milk, one which has been considered in the past, namely cheese. Seventy per cent of our cheese is marketed in Great Britain. I would presume that the policy followed would be something like this:	We will continue to
market 70 per cent of our cheese in Great Britain. Under our agreement we now have we will market more than 70 per cent. The agreement provides for a return which is just as high as we got during the last three years of which we spoke. The only adjustment, that is necessary is as related to the subsidy. The

Supply-Agriculture
price in the new agreement is the price we got for those three years. So that the floor is provided under cheese.
The position that has been dealt with through subsidies may also be provided for in certain agreements which are made. There is no necessity whatsoever for doing anything to put cheese under the floor prices measure.
One can apply the same principle to butter and to canned milk. When you have it applied to all those products it will have an influence upon fluid milk, and it is just possible that there will be no necessity for doing anything under the floor prices measure if we can maintain our contract and our supplies to Great Britain and to other countries. But if we are not able to maintain those floors, then we have the floor prices measure to utilize for the purpose, and it would be put into effect by the federal government.
It may require that we do like the prices board did. The prices board in making their operations effective utilized the services of the provincial milk boards. In dealing with some of these matters we may have to utilize the services of provincial organizations, too. I find that no one makes very much fuss about it, if you pay the money.
I understand that if the price is maintained for three years after the war, and was maintained for three years during the war, floor prices do not apply. Is that right?
So long as the prices remain up at satisfactory levels you do not need to apply any compulsion or even persuasion-so long as they remain up there. It may be for a longer period than three years.
One thing is certain, that if the two-cent subsidy on consumer milk is removed, somebody has to pay for it. Is it to be the consumer or the producer?
It will be the poor farmer.
That is the thing I should like to know. If it is to be the producer it will be too bad for him. On the other hand, if it is the consumer-
It will be too bad for him.
Yes. Who will bear it? That is an important question, and the minister should answer it.

I should like to compliment the minister upon having brought this matter before the committee so that it can be discussed. There is one thing about the Minister of Agriculture: He is never afraid to come to the house and to try to justify any action he takes. He is to be complimented upon that-even though I do not agree with him at this time. I think it is, indeed, a clever political move to turn back to the provinces the fight between the producer and the consumer, so far as prices are concerned.
They asked for it.

Some of them; not all of them. That is what this amounts to. The . Minister of Finance did not say what would happen when the producer subsidy on milk is withdrawn this fall. I understand that the producer subsidy will be taken off entirely on September 30. Then, are price ceilings, so far as milk is concerned, also to be lifted on September 30 when producer subsidies are taken off? Is the ceiling on whole milk to be taken off at that time too, and leave supply and demand to determine the price? Or are ceilings to be still kept on, and the farmer take the rap?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter of price will then be in the hands of the local boards.

Then the dominion government's price ceiling policy in regard to milk will be entirely taken off. There will be no ceilings at all, and on September 30 the matter will be entirely in the hands of provincial boards.

I explained that when I brought the question before the committee this afternoon. The announcement was made that we are taking off the consumer subsidy. That is the first part of it. The further announcement is made that the control over the price of milk, and the control of quotas and other things, is handed over to the provincial milk boards. Then we say-
Well, can I-

Just let me finish. Listen, and talk afterwards; and we shall probably understand one another when we are through.
Then, also, in order to give them four months to adjust the position as between the control of the prices board, and control by provincial boards, we are going to pay the highest subsidy on milk that we have ever paid, twenty cents higher than we ever paid before at any time in the summer. It is being raised from thirty-five to fifty-five cents. We will continue to pay that until September 30. In the meantime all this material in the minds of hon. members this evening will be discussed back and forth between the
Supply-Agriculture

authorities here and the provincial authorities, and some method will be found to deal with the situation. We hope that will be accomplished by October 1, and the whole control, from there on, will then pass over to the provincial authority.

I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Finance. There have been some misleading statements concerning this consumer subsidy on milk. The present price ceiling in Ottawa is ten cents. What will be the price ceiling in Ottawa as of June 1 this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be 12 cents.
What is the total amount of subsidy paid on farm products in the last five years?

I could answer that better when we are discussing subsidies generally. I have the information in this pile of material in front of me. I shall deal with it systematically when we go through the items one at a time. But it will take some time to dig it up.
I am probably out of order in anticipating-
Everybody is.

But, in considering this increase in the price of milk, I have been sitting here trying to anticipate what will happen to the incomes of old pensioners, persons living on annuities and on invested capital- small incomes. If we have the same thing in the field of milling, and make the consumer bear the cost of the subsidy on bread; and if we do the same thing with meat I am won faring what will happen. For instance, if we withdraw the freight subsidy and make the man who buys meat in Ontario bear the cost of freight, we shall have increased prices on milk, bread and meat, with the result that the person on a fixed income who is buying those necessities of life will be seriously handicapped in setting a table. I should like to know where we stand on this matter of subsidies.

That is all part and parcel of the discussions which have been going on for some years and which the Minister of Finance has < had to answer every time his estimates have been up. I suppose he will be prepared to discuss it again when they are up this year. It all concerns the question of inflation and whether we have come to the time when we should let this whole thing go back and have it a matter of bargaining between producer and consumer. If that is the

way it is going to be, we shall have the results that have been suggested sooner or later. We have said that it must be taken up in slow stages, that we must not go too fast with it, that we must try to make adjustments as we go along. In this case we have given four months in which we can try to make adjustments in a way that will not lower the returns to the producers or unduly increase the cost to the consumer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understood the committee to agree that there would not be a general discussion on price control.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I thought it was agreed the discussion would be only on price control in connection with dairy products. The item before the committee is 26, dairy products, $438,652. I would suggest that the discussion be relevant to that item. I understood that there was not to be a complete discussion to-night on this item, but that after there had been some discussion the item would stand and we would revert to item 5.
_Mr. ROSS (Souris): In view of the statements that have been made, could the Minister of Finance tell us approximately what the milk subsidy, both to the consumer and to the producer has cost annually?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The consumer subsidy cost from $20 million to $22 million this year, while the producer subsidy cost has been about $14 million. It will be understood that the producer subsidy is on the old basis that prevailed for the twelve months ended April 30, 1946.

Anything that I said a while ago was not in criticism of the government's price policy and I do not want to be misunderstood in that connection. I have said in my own constituency that I have not a great deal of criticism to make of the government's price policy. I realize they have had a tough problem and they have done a good job. I was merely suggesting that it was time they changed their policy in order to solve the problems that exist.
What effect will this announcement have upon the present price structure of the manufacture of cheese? I have had a number of letters from cheese manufacturers who say that since the subsidy was reduced some weeks ago they find it difficult to manufacture cheese and sell it at a profit.
There has been no reduction in the cheese subsidy.

In connection with the milk they have to buy.

Supply-Agriculture
Not for cheese.
Has the government had any correspondence with the provinces with respect to this matter? In making this announcement are they taking it for granted that the provinces will accept it?

There has been no direct discussion with the provincial governments in connection with the policy announced to-day, but there have been discussions with producers' and other organizations interested in the other side of the matter, that is, those who have been buying milk. There is another matter that I referred to when I made the announcement. I said that a decision had not been reached with regard to the subsidy to be paid on milk going into the production of cheese and that a decision has not been reached with regard to the subsidy to be paid on milk going into the production of canned milk. I stated that those decisions would be made within a few days.

After all this discussion the minister has cleared up one point that was not clear. I come from a dairy district and I own a dairy farm. I understood the minister to say that subsidies were off at a given date, September 30.
That is correct.
I understand that they are not off definitely as yet in so far as manufactured products are concerned.
We have been discussing fluid milk. They are all off in so far as fluid milk is concerned, but the question as to what is to be done in relation to cheese and canned milk is not yet determined.

I cannot understand how the provinces can set the price to be paid to the producer when they have absolutely no control over the selling price. The hon. member for Macleod brought up the point about the provincial governments being consulted. The money that is made, if any, on a dairy farm is made in the fluid milk market. Approximately sixty-five per cent of the milk has to go into the manufacturing market. As I understand it, we are now playing into the hands of a few independent shippers who sell fluid milk. We are saying to the provinces that they shall decide what the producers are to be paid and then we as a federal government say what it shall be sold at. As I understand the situation, that is not what was done when we were dealing with the struggling Massey-Harris Company; they were called in and asked what they could afford to produce at. I
should like to know whether the dairy council of Canada or the Canadian federation of agriculture were consulted before this policy was decided upon.

The Canadian federation of agriculture made their representations and the matter was discussed with them, I think just about the time the house met. It has been discussed with officials of the organization since that time. I am not suggesting that they have agreed to what has been done, the question has been discussed with them and their point of view obtained, as well as the point of view of many others.
Probably I did not make myself entirely clear, judging from one of the remarks made, with regard to the position in relation to cheese and canned products. The suggestion is made 65 per cent of the milk is marketed in that way in the Fraser river valley. Those are the two products in connection with which I said we have not yet determined what the subsidies will be, but any adjustments that are made will be upward. I made that statement this afternoon as part of my announcement. That is some indication of what it may be necessary to pay in connection with fluid milk if the fluid milk is to be obtained.
The minister said . that if any adjustments were made they would be upward. Can I take it from that that they will not be downward?
The hon. member certainly can. That is what that means.

The thought that occurred to me as I listened to the statements of the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance was, where does the government think it is going by this change except it be to save the $20,000,000 consumer subsidy and temporarily to continue the $14,000,000 producers subsidy. I do not see how consumers can derive any benefit from this change. They are to pay the price they paid in 1941, without the reduction that the subsidy represented. Consequently the people with large families who benefited from the consumers subsidy during the war years will be at a disadvantage by this change. One of the arguments used by the government in favour of the children's allowance was that it would assist the heads of large families' in buying necessities for the children. The government must have entirely forgotten their arguments of that time when they adopted the policy announced to-day.
There are three primary classes involved in this policy, namely the consumer, the distributor and the producer of milk. Let us forget
Supply-Agriculture

the distributor for the moment because he is to be allowed to charge to the public the 1941 ceiling price, instead of charging two cents of that to the government. There will have to be an adjustment between the distributor and the producer through the provincial milk control boards of the price paid by the distributor to the producer. The producer gets nothing from this change unless it be the extra twenty cents subsidy on the whole milk that is granted to him as of May 1. If he were to absorb the whole shock of the loss of the consumer subsidy he would lose about eighty cents per hundredweight on his milk. Thus he would have a net loss of sixty cents a hundredweight.
So we see that the dominion government have forgotten about the consumer. They are not caring about how cheaply the consumer can buy his milk. They are not caring very much about what the producer will be paid. They are throwing the squabble between the producer and the distributor to the milk boards and keeping on the ceiling price for some possible protection to the consumer. Is this facing the real situation that confronts Canada in connection with whole milk production?
How is this policy going to affect the diverting of whole milk into the production of cheese and other dairy products? Possibly it may enable the distributor to cut down the price to the producer so that the producer will sell his milk to the cheese factory or the butter creamery or for the manufacture of other by-products of whole milk. That may boost the production of butter and the production of cheese, but it certainly will not put the farmer in a better position to persuade his son or the returned soldier to come back and settle on the farm, nor will it relieve the farmer from sending his milch cows across to the United States for the better prices he gets there. It is certainly not going to have any effect on the production of beef unless it be by making the sale of whole milk less remunerative. To-day in this locality you do not need to go out into the country; all you need to do is to look in the daily papers, to see how many farms, farm stock and machinery are being sold by auction. There is only one explanation. The farmer would not be selling his stock and machinery and his farm if it were profitable for him to stay on his farm. The hon. member for New Westminster said that he knows something about farming because he has milked a cow, but it is the farmer who is selling off his stock and machinery and sending his milch cows across the border who knows whether he is getting a fair share of the national income.

I do not see how this change is going to help things. The Minister of Agriculture a few moments ago, to illustrate a point he was making, said that we should drive through the country and look at the dates on the buildings on the farms. I do not know what buildings he was talking of, because the farmer, in the first place, could not get the paint, even if he could afford it, to paint the date on a new building, let alone the labour or materials required to build. The Minister of Agriculture must admit that for fifteen years now, not just the last five years, farm buildings have not been improved to any degree. There was a shortage of farm improvements even before the war, in the depression days. When the price ceiling was set on the 1941 basis of prices, agriculture particularly was in an unfavourable position because agricultural prices had not risen to the same degree as manufactured goods, or as labour. The price of whole milk varied in different areas, even within the province. The mechanic who was good at repairing farm machinery is not now available to the farmers because he can get much higher wages and shorter hours in the city. The result of all this is that only a very small percentage of our returned men are going into agriculture.

Does my hon. friend
want the controls taken off or kept on?

I would certainly say that the dominion government to-day is keeping the control on the ceiling price and not on the equitable adjustment of prices to the producer. In arranging the price as between producer and distributor and consumer, nobody can now control the situation properly. I am one of those who believe that if price ceilings on agricultural products were removed it would be only a short time before these inequities would be eliminated. Then a proper price, instead of an artificial, unfair and unjust price would prevail, and our rural areas would not be denuded of labour for the farm. Let prices seek their own level, as they always have done. We have lived in a world where agriculture has carried on since the day the *world began. We did not have control until very recently, and we did not run into any panic that ever showed an unfair advantage to the agricultural producer as a result of accelerated prices. Consequently, as I look upon the announcement, I am at a loss to find out where there will be a benefit either to the consumer or to the primary producer. I cannot help concluding that the aim is entirely to benefit the coffers of the federal treasury at the expense of both the consumer and the primary producer.

Supply-Agriculture

I think it ought to be pointed out to all hon. members that the sum total of the result of all this discussion has pretty well established the idea that the subsidy ought to stay and that if it is removed at this time it will injure both the producer and the consumer. I believe the only reason why some of the Progressive Conservatives have not advocated the retention of the subsidy is that they recognize that they would not be able to continue to pay it themselves if they were in power and consequently they are afraid to make a commitment.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Boucher), it might be interesting for him to contemplate this question. Was the adjustment between consumer and producer prices fair and equitable in 1935 or 1936 or 1937 or 1938 or 1939 when none of these controls existed? I think he will find that it was not, that the adjustment was not satisfactory to anybody. People were not getting the milk; the milk was not being produced, and neither consumers nor producers were prosperous; all of which ought to indicate that the time has come in the history of the world and of this country when a far-reaching adjustment must be made in the whole financial system as it affects prices. The day has come when subsidies are here to stay, and they must stay if we are to be prosperous and happy and have adequate production.
I suggest that there must be an adjustment in the financial system which will enable us to get money without taking it out of the taxpayer's pockets. That money we can obtain as a result of the production of the country, and it can be used to finance subsidies, so that we shall be able to give a fair price to the consumer, such as he can pay, and a fair price to the producer, such as will enable him to carry on and produce buoyantly and with confidence.

I rise with great diffidence because I have not the good fortune to have spent the greater part of my life in agricultural pursuits, but I do have the privilege of representing an agricultural constituency and I am alarmed at receiving a copy of the local newspaper to-day telling me that the creamery at Nanaimo has ceased operation after it has been operating ever since 1906.
There is, in an editorial in the Nanaimo Free Press, an analysis of the difficulties under which one of the dairy farmers in that immediate vicinity had to operate, and if the minister has no objection I should like to read it to him. I think it shows the great difficulties of the dairy farmer on Vancouver island:
In no better way could the story of what has happened be told than through the medium of one dairyman's set of books, properly authenticated and vouched for. He has a place near East Wellington, is thoroughly experienced and a most careful and methodical operator. His figures cover statistics on five milking cows, two calves fed for seven weeks and two heifers fed and kept for a year's period. Total poundage produced include 200 pounds of milk for household, or home consumption was 46,300 pounds. Here is a segregation of his return, and also his operating expenses. He sold 41,100 pounds of milk at $1.80 per hundredweight. At seven weeks he sold his two calves for $55. He kept his two heifers and estimated their worth at $60 and he estimated the value of milk used in the household at $3.60. Thus his gross return for the year was $869.40.
Now come his operating expenses. He had to buy 15 tons of hay at $15 a ton, a total of $225; 20 tons of roots, mangels, carrots, turnips at $9 per ton, $180; a half-ton of milk feeds per month at $30 a ton, $180; his depreciation on the herd of five cows per year was marked off at $60; and three per cent interest on his investment of $5,000 was $150 . . . therefore his operating expenses were $785.
Deduct operating costs from cash returns and we find he was $84.40 ahead . . . providing of course he took nothing for the great amount of labour he had expended all year.
I suggest that it is not a very profitable or even a very exciting business for an older man, and for a younger man returning from the war it is not very attractive. The question I should like to ask is this. It may not be a sound question and if it is not I apologise. I believe there is some sort of subsidy paid on feed grains shipped from the prairie provinces to Vancouver island to assist dairy men in that part of the province.
We pay the freight.
Will that be removed?

We pay the freight from Calgary and Edmonton into British Columbia. It has no connection with this.
Item stands.
Science serviceo. Science service administration, $32,487.

I think it would be more logical if we took item 1 last and hon. members discussed on the various items the points in which they are interested. I am pleased to see in the items appearing under "science service" an increase of over $900,000. That is a step in the right direction, providing as it does for an increase in technical staff and some increase in salaries, which also is a step in the right direction.
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a problem which is of serious concern to the fruit growers of my constituency. I refer to the little cherry disease. This is a matter of concern to the people who grow,
Supply-Agriculture

and who without doubt have grown for years, the best cherries in Canada, people who have cleared forests and in many cases make a large portion of their living by the production of this fruit. I am glad to know from the science service officials that they are now going to pay specific and effective attention to the problem in the near future. I wish to make a few suggestions to the minister in this respect. This disease is giving us great concern in British Columbia. The science service, in cooperation with the provincial departments of agriculture and other bodies, have effected remedies for diseases over the years, but in each case the officials concerned have been greatly assisted by close cooperation with the growers. I would suggest to the minister that in this case he must get success at the earliest possible date. I realize it is a problem to discover the root cause of this virus disease which is threatening the cherry industry, and which is causing a great deal of concern to the province of British Columbia. Planting of new orchards is not taking place because the young trees are affected in the first year of growth. There must be close cooperation between the science service and the growers concerned.
We have a large number of men growing cherries in the district, and they have been doing so for many years. They have a great deal of experience and are capable of close observation of the growth and growing conditions. I would suggest to the minister that there should be periodical publicity in the districts concerned and reports made concerning the progress made from month to month. To solve this problem we must have the growers and the officials of the department working together in all parts of the district.
I would also sugges't that the officials of the department should take advantage of every opportunity they can to attend growers' meetings and explain in person to the growers what their plans, progress and problems are.
I have one other suggestion to make in this connection. This is a social problem in our district. The inspiration for rural education in rural schools should spring from the farm. There should be cooperation with the agricultural organizations of the district concerned, and there should be the cooperation of the high-school children, that is those who are of age to understand the investigation into this disease. In the past we have not related the daily education of the children directly enough to the problems that they will be expected to face if they are to remain on the farms. I throw out the suggestion to the officials of the department, that they try,

in cooperation with the agricultural organizations in the district, to have the senior pupils of the rural schools throughout the district interested in and playing a part in the solution of this problem.
I should like to ask the minister this question. What arrangements are being made for cooperation with the provincial department of agriculture in connection with investigation of this problem?

In the Kootenay valley the little cherry virus disease is spreading rapidly, having reached twenty miles north, fifteen miles west and forty-five miles south of where it was first observed in 1939. In 1941 its virus nature was demonstrated and investigations have been conducted under the directions of this department to try and determine what the origin is. I understand that there are some limited areas in the United States where they have had outbreaks of little cherry, but that there is little known about the disease, as to how it gets into a district or what is the cause of it; whether it is an insect, whether it is something in the air, or what it may be, has not been determined. We have three men who are working continuously in the Kootenay valley. Most of the work having to do with virus of different kinds is carried on at Summerland, but there is some hesitation to take the cherries that are affected into that district. It is a fruit-growing district that is not troubled with this fruit virus up to the present; and until the cause is known, some method of treating it, it is not being taken outside the valley for any purposes whatsoever. But we have three men in there who are working continuously on it, and it is hoped that we shall discover the causes and then be able to find some way of dealing with it. Up to the present we have not been able to discover any successful method of dealing with it.

I should like to make a few observations on a question which is closely associated with the production of food, namely, the conservation of food or the avoidance of waste. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made some remarks on the same subject early in the evening, but I deferred mine because I desired to get through with item 26.
This matter was greatly emphasized in my mind just the other day by observing the shocking waste of food that one can see in a great many public places in this country at the present time. I was in a restaurant, not in this city, the other day, and I was so shocked by what I saw that I made up my mind I would try to bring it to the attention

I should like to read one or two short extracts, upon which I wish to say a word. The first extract is from the New Statesman and Nation of April 20. It is as follows:

That is the quotation from the military authorities. Then the writer goes on to say:

I now wish to read an extract from Life, which is not usually regarded as a sentimentalist paper. It contains a few facts which are not new but I think are desirable for us to have before us. This copy of Life is dated May 6, and the quotation reads as follows:
An estimated 500 million persons in such countries as Italy and Greece, France and Germany, India, China and Japan were subsisting on 700 to 1,500 calories a day-not quite enough to die on but not enough to live on. I have one point to make. I think this needs to be dramatized to the people of Canada. With regard to the answer the minister gave me the other day in which he said, as I recall it, that he had O.K.'d an advertisement which is to be produced, I suggest that the government is not giving us a sufficient lead. I hope I am not putting this in a controversial way, because my desire is to persuade, not to criticize.
I have one further observation to make, and I shall point it up by reading a short extract from the New York Times of May 8. This is an editorial entitled "Hunger will not wait," 63260-102
and I should like to read the last paragraph because it has something to do not merely with humanity but with common sense:
Some world issues can be discussed at leisure. This one cannot. Hunger does not wait. This crisis is our opportunity to prove that we are not talking platitudes when we say we believe in world peace and world neighbourliness. These are our neighbours. They are hungry. A wave of good will and hope will sweep the world if now we share with them. It is time for leadership in this city and in the nation to turn from lesser things and show us how to do it.
I wish to make one final comment. A year ago to-day the Prime Minister, the hon. member for Peel and others were in San Francisco, and our hopes were high. Now I rub my eyes and ask myself if we are still living in the same world, when our hopes have shrivelled as they have. As I read this item in the New York Times, it suggests that at the present time we may create here and there sparks of good will which will kindle a generous flame which in turn may do something to melt, as it were, the freezing from which the whole world is suffering at the present time, and which seems to have destroyed the good will which existed a year ago.
So I suggest that whatever can be done by the government to give us a lead to that end will be worth while, and I believe the people of this country are the kind of people who will respond to such a lead.

May I add just one word by way of information, strangely enough relating to the subject of milk, about which we have heard so much to-night. We have heard of conditions in continental Europe and elsewhere,, and I should like to try to arouse some interest and perhaps do away with some of the complacency which sometimes exists with respect to the needs of these parts of the world. I am not dealing with Britain at the moment, because I intend to do so at a later time. In December of last year we were in Amiens, France, and were told by a high official of that city-and let the committee take note of this-that no adult civilian in the whole of that area, which has a huge population, had tasted a drink of milk for the past six years. With this observation I thought perhaps I might do something to arouse public interest and perhaps banish complacency in regard to what people in some parts of the world, allies of ouns, are going through in this critical period of peace.

I should like to say a few words in connection with the science of agriculture. I want to join with other hon. mem-

Supply-Agriculture

bers who have congratulated the minister upon the increase of $900,000 in the amount to be expended for the development of science in agriculture.

The increase in $913,591. I believe the application of science to Canadian agriculture might possibly solve one of the greatest problems confronting us. Up to the outbreak of the first world war it is fair to say the chief reason for producing agricultural commodities was to supply food for human consumption. There was a very good reason why that object should have kept people busy producing a livelihood. At the turn of the century one family working on the farm could produce sufficient food to supply one family living in the city; but owing to the application of mechanical methods to farming we have now reached the point, according to the United States department of agriculture, where one farm family can supply agricultural commodities sufficient for five families in the city.
At the present time there is no problem in regard to finding markets for agricultural commodities, but I think it fair to say that at some time in the near future we shall again reach the point where we shall have to look abroad for markets for our agricultural production ; and it would appear that the development of science or more properly the application of science to Canadian agriculture can do a great deal in solving that problem. That problem can be solved in this manner. Canadian agriculture can be made the basis for supplying raw materials to Canadian industry. Already that is being done to some extent in the United States. During the war years 275,000,000 bushels of United States wheat were converted into alcohol for industrial purposes. The same developments could be applied at the present time to Canadian agriculture. Only recently the national farm chemurgy council held a conference at St. Louis, Missouri. That conference expressed interest in the chemurgic plant of the Canadian government at. Saskatoon. It was also interested in this federal government's scientific research on our experimental farms. That conference went on record as stating that it would be the duty of United States scientists in the future to apply American agriculture to the production of the needs of American industry. In other words, they are going to try to make American agriculture the source of raw materials for American industry.
I should like to give some figures in that connection. The United States department of agriculture have told us that during the war
[Mr. Moore.1
years they lost five million people from the middle western states. Those people have gone to the eastern manufacturing centres, and to all intents and purposes will be lost to American agriculture. The American people are concerned with what is to be done to find a market for agricultural goods in that country; and I venture to say that people in Canada should be concerned too, because we are more dependent upon foreign markets for agricultural commodities, under ordinary peace-time conditions, than are the United States. In the late 1930's eighty-five per cent of American agricultural production was consumed in the home market. In Canada we do not consume anything like that percentage of our agricultural production.
There are a number of things which could be done from a scientific point of view to pave the way for the creation in this country of a market for agricultural commodities. First let us take the production of nylon in the United States. I hear some hon. member say, "Oh, oh." I admit that we do not produce any nylon in Canada, but we supply the materials from which it is produced. Fifty per cent of the cellulose used in the production of United States nylon comes from Canada in the form of wood pulp, and our pulpwood is running very, very short. Practically all products of the farm can be used to produce certain kinds of cellulose, and it would be a good thing for our scientific research department to go forward and see if it would not be possible to produce from the various forms of agricultural commodities sufficient cellulose to take care of the United States demand for our wood pulp used for this purpose.
There is something else we can consider doing. For instance, take the supply of fuel for internal combustion engines. There can be no question at all that the supply of fuel will become a serious matter in the not distant future. The United States supply of oil was used to a very large extent during the war years, and the American petroleum institute have told us that at the present time there is available in the United States 17 billion barrels of gasoline. At the present rate of consumption that will be consumed within fifteen years time. What are we going to do to supply some means of operating our internal combustion engines?
The best possible development would be to use ethyl alcohol produced from Canadian grain. The United States have told us that if we use a 10 per cent mixture of gasoline with ethyl alcohol, taking 1935 as a base, it would

require the total production of the 1935 wheat crop in the United States to produce the required amount of ethyl alcohol.
So if we care to put our scientists to work, and treat this problem as a national one, there is no reason why we cannot solve the problem confronting agriculture in Canada under peace-time conditions. It is well to speak of ordinary peace-time conditions, because the day will come in this country when we shall have to look elsewhere for more markets. The best place to look for agricultural markets in future will be to our own secondary industries, by supplying them with the raw materials they need to produce manufactured goods.
I should like to mention something else from the United States picture which could be done in Canada as well. During the year just ended the United States produced $100 million worth of goods out of agricultural products used for non-food purposes. That is the application of science to American agriculture. Plastics could be developed as well. Starches can be manufactured from agricultural goods. So also can anti-freeze and even edible syrups. The United States now have a plan to produce syrup from wheat, and in the production of that syrup they intend to use wheat which is not of the highest quality.

Up in Lambton county, on the shores of lake Erie, we grow corn for our silos, for husking and feeding purposes. A
few years ago we had a rigid corn-borer inspection. A new inspector was appointed and he started out as new brooms always do, the result being that five or six years ago we had a rigid inspection. But when the war came on we slipped a little, and for the last year or two we have not had a corn-borer inspection. The result is that the corn-borer is increasing quite rapidly. What is being done to restore the corn-borer inspection and to control this pest, if possible?

There has been some difficulty in getting staff in connection with the* work that is being done to control the corn-borer. I think it would be interesting if I read this statement on the European corn-borer :
The European corn-borer continues to be a serious pest of corn in Ontario and southern Quebec. During the season of 1945 this insect also made one ol its periodic invasions into New Brunswick, causing serious losses to corn, particularly in Carleton county. The development of a two-generation strain of the corn-borer in southwestern Ontario is threatening not only to complicate the control measures but increase the seriousness of the pest.
The normal single generation life-history of the insect is well known. The adult moths emerge from corn and other host plant refuse, begin flying and laying eggs in July. The larvae hatching from these eggs bore into the stalks and cobs of corn, feeding there until mature. They spend the winter in the host plant and weed refuse, pupate in the spring and emerge as adults early in July. The two-generation strain is not so well known. The first generation adults emerge in June and infest young corn plants, the larvae mature and pupate the same season. The second generation adults emerge late in the summer and infest the ripening corn.
In other words, a new variety of pest has appeared recently and is causing some difficulty in handling the situation. I am sorry I have no information As to why the inspector has not been on the job in Lambton county, other than that we have had difficulty in maintaining a competent staff.

In Kansas and other states where they were bothered with the corn-borer they maintained a patrol of the highways and stopped and searched all cars to make sure that they were not carrying com from the infested areas into free areas, and I understand that this helped greatly in eliminating the corn-borer. Something along that line will have to be done here.

In answer T.o a question that was asked with regard to control of forest insects by spraying from aircraft, I may say this. The application of concentrated sprays containing DDT from aircraft was first attempted in Canada in 1944. In that year, in cooperation with the Ontario department of lands and forests, several acres of balsam and spruce forest in Algonquin park, Ontario, were sprayed, plane owned and operated by the United States department of agriculture being employed. The results were sufficiently satisfactory to justify further experiments in 1945. Three separate spraying projects were conducted, all directed against the spruce budworm. At Algonquin park, ten experimental plots of ten acres each were sprayed in early May to determine the relative effeetivness of various dosages of DDT. In the Kakabonga region, Gatineau valley, Quebec, several experimental plots were sprayed between May 16 and June 14; the results from each series of sprays, employing varying dosages of DDT and solvent, were carefully checked by means of population studies taken in the sprayed plots and in adjacent unsprayed areas. The studies suggest that the most effective time to apply the spray is during the period in which the larvae are feeding on the foliage of the new growth. In the case of large-scale operations, however, when time is an important factor, spraying may be conducted in the needle-mining and bud-feeding stages but with increased dosages.
